summary.value: This paper proposes a backward-guided correction framework, SAC-Opt, to better utilize problem semantics to model optimization problems.

strengths.value:
- A semantically driven correction method was developed.
- The authors evaluated it on several different datasets.

weaknesses.value:
- As the article states, the authors cleaned all the evaluation sets, which raised a series of issues. For example, IndustryOR originally had 100 samples, but after cleaning, it only had 42 samples, less than half of the original size. But in Table 1, the authors directly cited other people's results for comparison; is this fair? I checked the repository of Xiao et al. (2025)'s article (https://github.com/LLM4OR/LLM4OR) and found that the IndustryOR test set still maintains 100 test data points. The authors need to carefully check the rigor of their experiments.
- In Table 1, SAC-Opt shows an IndustryOR of 63.7%, but no figure divided by 42 yields this result. How was this figure calculated? How many of the 42 questions were answered correctly? Similarly, the reproduction rates of 44.0% for OptiMUS-0.2 and 54.0% for OptiMUS-0.3 are unexplained. Therefore, **I seriously doubt the validity of the entire Table 1 and indeed all the experimental results presented in this paper**.
- Similarly, of the 211 samples in the ComplexLP dataset, only 111 were retained, nearly half were removed. These complex datasets have been processed, but detailed explanations are lacking. Are the authors avoiding the problem that SAC-OPT is unsuitable for solving?
- Solving optimization problems using large models is a hot topic, and authors should make a comprehensive comparison with the latest work in the field, such as LLMOPT, OptMATH, SIRL, ORLM, etc.
- Does gradual convergence lead to a longer time to obtain the answer? How to efficiently obtain a better answer should be evaluated.
- In line 34, Pyomo appears to be a modeling language rather than a solver.

**W1&W3：As the article states, the authors cleaned all the evaluation sets, which raised a series of issues. For example, IndustryOR originally had 100 samples, but after cleaning, it only had 42 samples, less than half of the original size. But in Table 1, the authors directly cited other people's results for comparison; is this fair? I checked the repository of Xiao et al. (2025)'s article (https://github.com/LLM4OR/LLM4OR) and found that the IndustryOR test set still maintains 100 test data points. The authors need to carefully check the rigor of their experiments. Similarly, of the 211 samples in the ComplexLP dataset, only 111 were retained, nearly half were removed. These complex datasets have been processed, but detailed explanations are lacking. Are the authors avoiding the problem that SAC-OPT is unsuitable for solving?**

We sincerely thank the reviewer for the careful examination of our evaluation setup. We clarify that our work does not perform any data cleaning. As clearly stated in Sec. 4.1 of our paper:
> "To ensure consistency, we adopt the cleaned and standardized versions provided by the survey Xiao et al. (2025) for all methods."

**! The reduced dataset sizes originate entirey from Xiao et al. (2025), not from our processing.**

The IJCAI survey conducted a thorough expert-based cleaning procedure. They reported:
> "11 human experts manually identify errors in the problems, and each error case is cross-validated by at least three different experts. We curate a cleaned and unified set of optimization modeling benchmarks.”

The publicly released cleaned benchmarks in their repository contain exactly the sizes mentioned by the reviewer, including 42 instances for IndustryOR and 111 for ComplexLP. We directly use these official cleaned datasets https://github.com/LLM4OR/LLM4OR/tree/master/static/clean_benchmarks
 without any modification.

**! Our comparisons are fully fair because all baselines are evaluated on the same cleaned benchmarks.**

In Xiao et al. (2025), their *own* experimental results (Table 2) are explicitly reported on the cleaned benchmark, as indicated in the table title:
> "Performance comparison of existing fully open-source methods **on cleaned benchmarks**."

Thus, every method in our comparison uses exactly the same dataset versions.

**! We are not avoiding difficult instances.**

We respectfully disagree with the reviewer's concern that the cleaned datasets might remove cases challenging for our method. All removals were performed by the survey authors using their multi-expert validation process prior to our work. The cleaned benchmark has become the standard evaluation setting in this research line, and we evaluate on every instance included in that official release.

Similarly, the reproduction rates of 44.0% for OptiMUS-0.2 and 54.0% for OptiMUS-0.3 are unexplained. Therefore, I seriously doubt the validity of the entire Table 1 and indeed all the experimental results presented in this paper.**

We sincerely thank the reviewer for the careful and thorough examination of our results. Your comment was extremely helpful, and we genuinely appreciate the opportunity to clarify and correct this issue.

After receiving your feedback, we conducted a careful re-audit of our log files. We discovered that, for the IndustryOR dataset, we mistakenly aggregated only four completed runs instead of the intended five. These four runs contained 27, 25, 26, and 29 correct predictions (out of 42), and the originally reported 63.7% was the average accuracy over these four runs. This was a clear oversight on our part, and we sincerely apologize for the confusion it caused.

During the re-audit, we also identified the same inconsistency in the reported results for OptiMUS-0.2 and OptiMUS-0.3. We have now carefully corrected all affected results. The missing fifth run for IndustryOR has been completed under identical settings, and the corresponding tables and descriptions have been updated accordingly. In addition, we manually reviewed all remaining datasets and runs one by one and confirmed that no further inconsistencies were present.

The corrected manuscript, which now includes the updated Table 1 and all related experimental sections, has been uploaded for the reviewer's inspection. To further improve transparency, we have added an extended statistical analysis of accuracy in Appendix A.9. We have also open-sourced the complete code to ensure full reproducibility. We would like to reassure the reviewer that, after these corrections, all main conclusions of our work remain unchanged.

We are truly grateful for the reviewer's diligence, which has greatly improved the accuracy and clarity of our experimental reporting. If any additional information or clarification would be helpful, we would be very happy to provide it.

**W4: Solving optimization problems using large models is a hot topic, and authors should make a comprehensive comparison with the latest work in the field, such as LLMOPT, OptMATH, SIRL, ORLM, etc.**

We thank the reviewer for this helpful comment. The recent survey by Xiao et al. (2025) [1] provides a clear taxonomy of existing approaches, distinguishing domain-specific LLMs, advanced inference frameworks, and benchmark datasets and evaluation. As noted in the second paragraph of the Introduction, "Our work builds on the inference framework line", and as stated in the Abstract, our method operates "without requiring additional training or supervision".

The methods mentioned by the reviewer, such as LLMOPT, OptMATH, SIRL, and ORLM, primarily focus on domains where models are trained or fine-tuned to improve optimization modeling performance. These methods therefore fall into other branches  such as domain-specific LLMs described in the survey, rather than the inference-framework line that our work investigates. For this reason they are not directly comparable in our setting.

**W5: Does gradual convergence lead to a longer time to obtain the answer? How to efficiently obtain a better answer should be evaluated.**

We thank the reviewer for the insightful question. It is correct that iterative correction may introduce additional computation. As discussed in Appendix A.4 (Discussion of Convergence) and Appendix A.8 (Run Time Comparison), we provide a detailed analysis showing that SAC-Opt converges in only a small number of iterations in practice and that the overall runtime overhead remains modest across datasets.

Table 5 further shows that SAC-Opt not only achieves notably higher modeling accuracy but also maintains runtime that is comparable to, and in some cases even lower than, the best baseline methods. We agree that exploring even more efficient strategies for obtaining high-quality solutions is valuable. Investigating lighter verification mechanisms or adaptive stopping criteria is a promising direction for future work.

**W6: In line 34, Pyomo appears to be a modeling language rather than a solver.**

We thank the reviewer for pointing this out. The reviewer is correct that Pyomo is a modeling language rather than a solver, and our original wording was not accurate. We have corrected this statement in the manuscript and uploaded the revised version accordingly.


References:

[1] Xiao, Ziyang, et al. "A Survey of Optimization Modeling Meets LLMs: Progress and Future Directions." In IJCAI, 2025.

summary.value: The paper proposes SAC-Opt, a semantics-anchored, backward correction framework for translating natural-language optimization problems into solver-executable code. The method first extracts structured elements (parameters, variables, constraints, objective), generates an initial program, and then iteratively reconstructs "semantic anchors" from the code to compare against the originals; only misaligned components are regenerated until alignment or a cap on iterations is reached. Empirically, across seven public datasets, SAC-Opt reports an average +7.8% absolute gain in modeling accuracy and up to +21.9% on ComplexLP, with ablations, cross-LLM generalization, and verification strategy comparisons. The paper provides prompt details and a reproducibility statement.

strengths.value:
- The paper shows how solver-driven debugging misses semantic mistakes and frames a backward, semantics-first loop to detect them. The end-to-end workflow is clearly depicted.  The introduction concretely illustrates semantic failure modes (e.g., "upper bound" encoded as "lower bound"). The decomposition into structured vs. semantic components reduces cumulative translation errors.

-  The core mechanism is well-specified, including formalization of reconstruction, verification, and correction. Two verification instantiations (LLM-based and similarity-based) operationalize semantic equivalence. Concrete prompts for reconstruction and verification are provided.

- Across seven datasets, SAC-Opt attains best accuracy with large gains on difficult sets (e.g., +21.9% on ComplexLP). Ablations isolate the effect of semantic correction vs. solver debugging; removing correction causes substantial drops. Cross-LLM generalization indicates benefits even with weaker backbones. Verification strategy comparison shows LLM-based checking is more accurate/efficient than similarity-based alternatives.

weaknesses.value:
- The "first semantics-driven correction method" claim in the Contributions is strong but not substantiated with a systematic comparison against other semantics-aware correction lines. 

- The Related Work section lists many inference frameworks but does not explicitly rule out semantics-driven correction precedents.

- The paper's empirical comparisons focus on method families but do not include a semantics-anchoring baseline beyond the two \delta instantiations internal to SAC-Opt. 

- Convergence is evidenced via a single-case error-set plot; no conditions on \delta, regeneration policy, or anchor space guarantee monotonic decrease or termination beyond a hard cap. Operation "M ← Msimp + M(t)sem" is not formalized. Composition boundaries between deterministic and regenerated segments are not precisely specified.

- Table 1 includes starred results imported from prior work; while stated to be under the same setting, such reuse can mask differences in extraction, prompting, or seeds. 

- Although the paper averages over five runs, Table 1 reports no dispersion; only Table 4 includes mean and std for internal variants. (Sec. 4.4, p.7–8; Table 4, p.8.) Why it matters: statistical robustness is unclear. :contentReference[oaicite:39]{index=39} 

- SAC-Opt increases runtime vs. the best baseline on several datasets. Average per-instance runtimes for SAC-Opt-LLM exceed many simple inference baselines in Table 7. (Table 7, p.18.) 

- The approach assumes reliable anchor extraction and adopts an external pipeline. Reported manual checks cover three datasets and suggest high extraction accuracy, but do not explore adversarial or systematic extraction errors. No controlled stress test perturbs anchor quality to quantify SAC-Opt’s tolerance.

comment.value:
**W1: The "first semantics-driven correction method" claim in the Contributions is strong but not substantiated with a systematic comparison against other semantics-aware correction lines.**

Thank you for pointing this out. We agree that the original wording was stronger than necessary and have revised it for clarity. Existing LLM-based optimization modeling methods rely on single-pass generation or solver-based correction, but none reconstruct semantics from generated code or align them with explicit semantic anchors. SAC-Opt introduces the first iterative backward correction loop at the semantic anchor level, enabling the detection and correction of semantic mismatches that prior approaches cannot reveal. We have updated the Contributions and Related Work sections to make this distinction clear.

**W2: The Related Work section lists many inference frameworks but does not explicitly rule out semantics-driven correction precedents.**

Thank you for the comment. In the revised version of *Sec. 2.2 CORRECTION IN OPTIMIZATION*, we add a concise clarification explaining that prior correction methods focus on extraction refinement or solver-based debugging, and do not reconstruct semantics from generated code or perform anchor-level alignment. Stating these distinctions explicitly helps make the contribution of SAC-Opt clear.

**W3: The paper's empirical comparisons focus on method families but do not include a semantics-anchoring baseline beyond the two \delta instantiations internal to SAC-Opt.**

Thank you for the comment. There is currently no published method that performs anchor-level semantic correction, so a direct semantics-anchoring baseline does not exist. Our experiments therefore isolate the contribution of semantic anchoring through internal comparisons. The w/o-correction setting in Table 2 removes the anchor loop entirely, reflecting forward pipelines in prior work, and the two $\delta$ variants in Table 4 test different semantic-checking mechanisms under the same protocol. We will make this rationale explicit in the revision.

**W4: Convergence is evidenced via a single-case error-set plot; no conditions on \delta, regeneration policy, or anchor space guarantee monotonic decrease or termination beyond a hard cap. Operation "M ← Msimp + M(t)sem" is not formalized. Composition boundaries between deterministic and regenerated segments are not precisely specified.**

Thank you for the insightful comment. In this work, convergence is defined as achieving semantic alignment, where all anchors are correctly represented. We agree that the current version does not provide theoretical proof to guarantee monotonic decrease. Our aim is to provide a practical alignment procedure rather than a formal convergence theorem. To ensure well-defined termination, SAC-Opt adopts a fixed iteration budget and a regeneration policy that only updates the anchors identified as misaligned in each step. This makes the update rule explicit and ensures that the procedure always halts after a pre-defined number of iterations. Empirically, this policy leads to consistent reductions in misaligned anchors across tasks, as shown in Table 4. We will clarify these points in the revised version so that the scope and meaning of "convergence" in our setting are more precisely stated.

Regarding the formalization issues, we agree that the operation $\mathcal{M} \gets \mathcal{M} _ {\mathrm{simp}} + \mathcal{M} _ {\mathrm{sem}}^{(t)}$ and the composition boundaries were not explained with sufficient clarity. In the revision, we clarify in Sec. 3.5 how the regenerated semantic components are merged with the deterministic parts of the model. We also describe in Sec. 3.3 that $\mathcal{M} _ {\mathrm{simp}}$ consists of parameters and variables that are deterministically rendered, while $\mathcal{M} _ {\mathrm{sem}}$ includes constraints and the objective, which encode the key logic and require regeneration. These clarifications make the regeneration process and model composition more precise.

**W5: Table 1 includes starred results imported from prior work; while stated to be under the same setting, such reuse can mask differences in extraction, prompting, or seeds.**

Thank you for raising this concern. The prior work from which the starred results are taken does not provide open-source code, so we rely on the numbers reported in the paper. To ensure fairness, we evaluate our experiments under the same protocol used in that work to the greatest extent possible. All other baselines are re-run by us using the same dataset, the same extraction pipeline, the same backbone model (GPT-4o), and fixed seeds. This keeps all controllable factors aligned and ensures that comparisons are made under a consistent evaluation setting. We have clarified this in Sec. 4.3 and updated the caption of Table 1 to clearly distinguish imported results from those reproduced under our unified protocol.

**W6: Although the paper averages over five runs, Table 1 reports no dispersion; only Table 4 includes mean and std for internal variants. (Sec. 4.4, p.7–8; Table 4, p.8.) Why it matters: statistical robustness is unclear.**

Thank you for pointing this out. Following the evaluation protocol commonly used in recent work [1,2], we report the five-run averages in Table 1 to ensure consistency with prior results and to make the comparison directly comparable to existing baselines, which are also presented without dispersion. Table 4 already includes mean and standard deviation for our $\delta$ variants under the same setup. To further improve clarity, we have added an extended statistical analysis of accuracy in Appendix A.9.

**W7: SAC-Opt increases runtime vs. the best baseline on several datasets. Average per-instance runtimes for SAC-Opt-LLM exceed many simple inference baselines in Table 7. (Table 7, p.18.)**

Thank you for the observation. As shown in Table 5, the overall runtime overhead of SAC-Opt relative to the best baseline is modest and in some cases, such as IndustryOR and ComplexOR, even lower. Appendix A.8 provides a detailed breakdown of average run time for all methods. This reflects a clear performance-cost trade-off: methods such as Standard, CAFA and Reflexion are indeed faster, but their accuracy is substantially lower and often insufficient for practical use. Our primary goal is to improve correctness, and the additional runtime of SAC-Opt is justified by the accuracy gains it achieves. We will make this trade-off explicit in the main text so that readers can clearly see both the accuracy improvements and their computational cost.

**W8: The approach assumes reliable anchor extraction and adopts an external pipeline. Reported manual checks cover three datasets and suggest high extraction accuracy, but do not explore adversarial or systematic extraction errors. No controlled stress test perturbs anchor quality to quantify SAC-Opt’s tolerance.**

Thank you for raising this important point. We agree that reliable anchor extraction is fundamental and that extraction errors can affect downstream modeling. Since extraction is not the focus of this work, we adopt the state-of-the-art OptiMUS-0.3 [3] pipeline to ensure consistent and strong input quality across all methods, so that our comparisons reflect modeling ability rather than variations in extraction. We manually checked samples from three datasets and observed high extraction accuracy, but this does not replace a systematic stress test. We have added this limitation to Appendix A.6 and identified controlled perturbation of anchor quality as a meaningful direction for future work.


References:

[1] Xiao, Ziyang, et al. "A Survey of Optimization Modeling Meets LLMs: Progress and Future Directions." In IJCAI, 2025.

[2] Xiao, Ziyang, et al. "Chain-of-experts: When llms meet complex operations research problems." In ICLR, 2024.

[3] AhmadiTeshnizi, Ali, et al. "OptiMUS-0.3: Using large language models to model and solve optimization problems at scale." arXiv preprint arXiv:2407.19633 (2024).

summary.value:
This paper is about turning problem descriptions given in text to optimization models (like TSP) to be solved by mixed-integer programming solvers (like Cplex, Gurobi).

The main angle of the paper is the introduction of SAC-Opt which focuses on "semantic" correctness of the constraint model along with execution correctness of the code. 

The idea is to go from text to constraint and then back; constraint to text, which allows comparing the initial text VS. generated text to have a proxy of semantic correctness. In this step, the paper proposes two methods: an LLM used as a judge for a binary agree/disagree decision and sentence similarity to detect same/not-same within some embedding distance threshold. Mismatches are corrected and the process is repeated in a loop until alignment is achieved on all constraints or iteration limit. 

The overall setup is heavily based on structured data initially generated from the given problem description text.

Experiments on existing datasets and methods show ~7% average improvement.

strengths.value:
- A study on semantic-correction is a nice addition to natural language to optimization model translation.
- The paper write-up is clear (though I have a few suggestions below) 
- Experiments show added value of semantic correction (albeit at the expense of runtime)
- Shares code/data which seems reproducible --thank you!

weaknesses.value:
My main concern with the paper is: the significance is not clear with respect to ICLR. 

Overall, I like this paper and it is a nice addition to an emerging array of approaches to NL4Opt. That said, the fact that adding more verification improves the correct code generation is somewhat expected, no? Here, we are looking at a %7 increase (notice most of that comes from one dataset with 21% improvement when averaged). Btw, what does this mean? Are we solving 1 or 2 (or 10) more problems correctly? It would be nice to quantify that in the number of problems to better understand the impact. So an expected improvement (at the expense of heavier approach, higher runtime) with marginal improvement.

The other thing is; the semantic verification step is an LLM detecting an inconsistency by looking at the backward step (constraint to text). I like the simplicity of this (again, at time/query expense) but what do we learn from an AI/ICLR point of view? So the overall contribution is the framework. Given the existing several frameworks, this specific improvement would be an excellent contribution, say at INFORMS. 

Other (minor) comments: 
- The presentation is clear but it fails in one important aspect. How does the re-generation works? This is one of the most important steps of the framework so I am surprised it is not explained in more detail. So say a constraint generation is detected for inconsistency. Then what happens? Do we present the LLM with the previous version and say that it's incorrect and point the incorrect example and why so? Or, something else? Most importantly, is there some "learning" here feeds back into the next generation. This is important details that must be explained in more detail. 

- It is not clear to me why the semantic verification step comes before the code verification. Code verification is easier/cheaper, no? Cannot you just run the code verification and ONLY IF it succeeds proceed with semantic verification. In the current form, this choice seems quite arbitrary. Consider an ablation. 

- Similar semantic loops are discussed as early as 2023, see e.g., the NL4Opt blueprint of Holy Grail 2.0 which is not cited https://arxiv.org/pdf/2308.01589 (btw, here the semantic step like MUS verification comes after the code verification) 

- The extract agents here is exactly "Ner4Opt" which is unfortunately not cited. pls fix. 
https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10601-024-09376-5 

- The authors rightly point out the annotation contamination in their experimental datasets and referred to a "cleaned" version (thank you!). Consider citing & using Text2Zinc, which also fixes these annotation leakage issue in test datasets. 
https://arxiv.org/pdf/2503.10642

- The higher runtimes are only disclosed in the appendix. Please be more up front about it in the main paper. 

- Similarly, there is a heavy dependency on structured extraction being correct in the first place. Please be more up front about this dependency in the paper. IF extraction does not work, the rest will not matter (and plz correct me if I am correct). In Appendix, there is a comment that it actually does work well, so that seems to work in practice (OR.. the datasets are easy) 

- The experiments jump to direct results on "x% improvement". What I would have liked more is a detailed analysis/statistics on the whole pipeline. In how many problems, the extraction works perfect. In how many it fails? And by how much? Rather a binary works/not-works, how many parameters/constraints it omits, how often? Then, for how many of those the initial generation is deemed incorrect by the LLM backward verification? Is that correct at all times, OR is there a case LLM semantics, itself, is incorrect? Then, how many loops are needed to fix it. Etc. etc.. I think there is a great empirical story/study that remains untold here, and that's more interesting than getting +1 more problem modelled correctly (these problems are easy to model anyways..). But even than, that's a niche study better fit for an optimization journal.

- Curiosity question; how did you tune/decide similarity threshold? 

- The paper says that this process converge, but I don't see why (without better understanding the re-generation step)

- There are a few places with the claim "model-agnostic". Are you referring to constraint models (as in swab Gurobi with Cplex) or LLM models. IF llm models, is not this obvious? We can feed in the prompt to LLM-A or LLM-B. This seems trivial to me so I am not sure why the paper is making this claim. Do you mean you found "universal prompts" (by some definition) that works for all LLMs? I am not really following this part. Please revise (or better, drop that part)

- I really do like the paper but what do we learn from AI/ICLR point of view? (in the light of several works have done this already)

The core innovation of our work is the introduction of semantic anchors as explicit and verifiable representations of modeling intent, together with a **backward semantic-level correction mechanism** that reconstructs semantics from the generated code and directly compares it with the intended anchors. Existing approaches, including multi-agent frameworks and solver-guided correction, operate purely in the forward direction and cannot detect silent semantic errors once the code becomes syntactically valid. SAC-Opt fundamentally differs from these methods by making intent explicit and machine-checkable, and by iteratively correcting only the misaligned components. This fills a long-standing gap in prior work, where subtle semantic mistakes introduced early in the pipeline remain unnoticed and unfixable.

As a result of this backward semantic-level correction, SAC-Opt substantially improves the reliability of natural-language modeling by ensuring that the generated solver code truly reflects the intended semantics. The ability to surface previously undetectable errors leads to clear gains on problems where existing pipelines consistently fail, especially on complex tasks. The method remains stable across different LLMs and datasets, indicating that semantic anchoring forms a broadly applicable strategy rather than a model-specific trick. We believe this demonstrates a direction of interest to ICLR: strengthening LLM reasoning through explicit semantic verification, and showing how backward alignment can enhance the robustness and generality of LLM-driven optimization modeling.

**W01: Overall, I like this paper and it is a nice addition to an emerging array of approaches to NL4Opt. That said, the fact that adding more verification improves the correct code generation is somewhat expected, no? Here, we are looking at a %7 increase (notice most of that comes from one dataset with 21% improvement when averaged). Btw, what does this mean? Are we solving 1 or 2 (or 10) more problems correctly? It would be nice to quantify that in the number of problems to better understand the impact. So an expected improvement (at the expense of heavier approach, higher runtime) with marginal improvement.**

Thank you for the comment. First, our goal is not to increase verification volume, but to detect semantic inconsistencies that current forward and solver-based methods cannot observe. The backward semantic alignment is designed specifically for revealing these silent errors, rather than adding heavier verification for its own sake. Second, the accuracy percentage and the number of correctly solved problems are fully aligned under the standard NL4Opt evaluation protocol, which is also used in prior work such as [1,2,3,4]. This is the common and accepted way to quantify correctness in this area. Third, Table 5 further reports both accuracy and runtime compared with the strongest baseline. The results show that SAC-Opt offers a good trade off, with clear gains on hard datasets and modest overhead. These findings confirm that SAC-Opt is effective and efficient, providing robust convergence and substantial improvements even on challenging optimization problems.

This is one of the most important steps of the framework so I am surprised it is not explained in more detail. So say a constraint generation is detected for inconsistency. Then what happens? Do we present the LLM with the previous version and say that it's incorrect and point the incorrect example and why so? Or, something else? Most importantly, is there some "learning" here feeds back into the next generation. This is important details that must be explained in more detail. Can you say more about re-generation step once inconsistencies are found? This is a crucial step of the paper that I am surprised not discussed in more detail?**

Thank you for raising this important question. After extracting the semantic anchors, SAC-Opt regenerates the code for each anchor using the semantic translation step described in Sec. 3.3. The generated code is then converted into a reconstructed semantic anchor following Sec. 3.4, and we check whether the reconstructed anchor matches the original one. If inconsistency is detected, the system simply repeats the same generation-reconstruction-verification cycle until alignment is achieved or the iteration limit is reached. We will expand Sec. 3 in the final version to describe this regeneration loop more explicitly, and Sec. 4.9 provides a concrete example illustrating how a semantic anchor is corrected.

Regarding whether the LLM receives the previous incorrect version or explicit feedback, the current design does not use historical information. This choice ensures simplicity and comparability between the two verification strategies we implement, since similarity-based verification cannot track past context. Despite its simplicity, Table 4 shows that SAC-Opt typically converges within a small number of iterations and remains stable across datasets. We fully agree that incorporating prior failure signals could further improve correction efficiency, and we are grateful to the reviewer for pointing out this valuable direction for future work.

**W2: It is not clear to me why the semantic verification step comes before the code verification. Code verification is easier/cheaper, no? Cannot you just run the code verification and ONLY IF it succeeds proceed with semantic verification. In the current form, this choice seems quite arbitrary. Consider an ablation.**

Thank you for raising this important point. We agree that solver-based code verification is cheaper, but the central problem our work addresses is different. Many semantic errors remain hidden in code that executes without any solver warnings, such as reversed inequality directions or missing terms. These errors are syntactically valid and therefore cannot be detected by code verification. Since our goal is to correct exactly these undetected semantic mismatches, semantic verification needs to be performed first.

Code verification still plays an important role, and we always apply it after semantic alignment to ensure that the final program is executable. The two forms of verification serve different purposes, and their order does not change the fact that semantic errors cannot be revealed through solver feedback alone. We appreciate the suggestion of evaluating alternative orders and will explore this direction in future work.

**W3: Similar semantic loops are discussed as early as 2023, see e.g., the NL4Opt blueprint of Holy Grail 2.0 which is not cited https://arxiv.org/pdf/2308.01589 (btw, here the semantic step like MUS verification comes after the code verification)**

Thank you for pointing us to Holy Grail 2.0. We have carefully read and cited this work. While it discusses a loop pipeline, its mechanism operates in a fundamentally different way. In Holy Grail 2.0, the checking is performed after code verification, and the refinement process relies on MUS-style diagnostics together with human validation. This procedure detects issues only after code execution and depends on user guidance during the correction stage. By contrast, SAC-Opt shifts the checking to an earlier, purely semantic stage, enabling it to detect and correct silent semantic mismatches *before* execution, including those that would never be surfaced by solver diagnostics. More importantly, our goal is to build a fully automatic and low-cost pipeline that minimizes human involvement and lowers the barrier of optimization modeling. SAC-Opt performs all semantic checks and corrections without manual intervention, enabling scalable and consistent semantic alignment that is not supported by prior approaches.

**W4: The extract agents here is exactly "Ner4Opt" which is unfortunately not cited. pls fix. https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10601-024-09376-5**

Thank you for pointing this out. Our extraction module follows the state-of-the-art approach introduced in OptiMUS-0.3 [4], which leverages reflective prompting and confidence-based feedback to ensure high-quality inputs. All experiments in our study rely on this same extraction pipeline to enable fair and controlled comparisons. We have now added a citation to Ner4Opt in the revised version, as it also investigates related extraction ideas.

**W5: The authors rightly point out the annotation contamination in their experimental datasets and referred to a "cleaned" version (thank you!). Consider citing & using Text2Zinc, which also fixes these annotation leakage issue in test datasets. https://arxiv.org/pdf/2503.10642**

Thank you for the suggestion. Our experiments already use the cleaned dataset provided in [1], which removes annotation leakage and ensures reliable evaluation. We have also added a citation to Text2Zinc in the revised version, as it similarly addresses annotation contamination issues in datasets.

**W6: The higher runtimes are only disclosed in the appendix. Please be more up front about it in the main paper.**

Thank you for the suggestion. We agree that the runtime overhead should be made more visible. In the revised version, we have moved the key runtime results from the appendix to the main paper and added a brief discussion to clearly present the trade-off between correction accuracy and computational cost.

**W7: Similarly, there is a heavy dependency on structured extraction being correct in the first place. Please be more up front about this dependency in the paper. IF extraction does not work, the rest will not matter (and plz correct me if I am correct). In Appendix, there is a comment that it actually does work well, so that seems to work in practice (OR.. the datasets are easy)**

We agree that structured extraction quality is foundational, and errors at this stage can influence downstream modeling. While SAC-Opt does not aim to solve extraction itself, it is designed to *detect and correct semantic inconsistencies after extraction* through iterative alignment with the original intent. To ensure strong and consistent input quality, we follow the state-of-the-art OptiMUS-0.3 [4] extraction pipeline across all methods, so differences in performance reflect modeling ability rather than extraction variance.

As detailed in Appendix A.6, manual review on the three complex datasets shows extraction accuracy already above 94%, and almost all semantic anchors (constraints/objective) are extracted correctly. For simpler datasets, large-scale manual checking is infeasible, but the very high final modeling accuracies (e.g., 96.5% on EasyLP in Table 1) imply extraction accuracy is even higher, since modeling accuracy cannot exceed extraction accuracy. These results indicate that extraction works reliably in practice and SAC-Opt remains robust even with small extraction imperfections. We will move this section from the appendix to the main paper if the pages allowed.

comment.value:
**W8: The experiments jump to direct results on "x% improvement". What I would have liked more is a detailed analysis/statistics on the whole pipeline. In how many problems, the extraction works perfect. In how many it fails? And by how much? Rather a binary works/not-works, how many parameters/constraints it omits, how often? Then, for how many of those the initial generation is deemed incorrect by the LLM backward verification? Is that correct at all times, OR is there a case LLM semantics, itself, is incorrect? Then, how many loops are needed to fix it. Etc. etc.. I think there is a great empirical story/study that remains untold here, and that's more interesting than getting +1 more problem modelled correctly (these problems are easy to model anyways..). But even than, that's a niche study better fit for an optimization journal.**

Thank you for this very helpful comment. We agree that a detailed analysis of the entire pipeline would provide deeper insight into how each component behaves. In this work, we follow the evaluation practice commonly used in current research so that our results remain directly comparable to prior studies [1,2,3,4]. Since extraction is not the main focus of SAC-Opt, we adopt the widely used OptiMUS-0.3 [4] extraction pipeline to keep input quality consistent across all methods. This allows the performance differences to reflect the modeling and correction capability of each approach rather than variations in extraction. As reported in the paper, we also manually checked extraction outputs on three datasets and observed high accuracy, although this is not a full investigation of possible error patterns.

The reviewer asked about the correctness of backward verification and the number of iterations needed for correction. These points are analyzed in Sec. 4.7 and Table 4. We report both the number of semantic correction rounds and the number of debugging rounds triggered by verification. This shows how often the verifier identifies a mismatch and how SAC-Opt resolves it during the alignment process.

We agree that a more complete study would also examine how often extraction fails, how large such failures are, how reliable the backward verification is in more challenging cases, and how the number of iterations changes when anchor quality is perturbed. To take a first step in this direction, we have added an extended statistical analysis of accuracy in Appendix A.9. A systematic stress test that explores extraction noise, verification reliability and correction dynamics is an important direction for future work.

**W9: Curiosity question; how did you tune/decide similarity threshold?**

Thank you for the question. We follow common practice and set the similarity threshold to 0.75, which offers a reasonable balance in practice. As noted in Sec. 4.7, similarity-based verification is consistently inferior to our LLM-based verifier in both accuracy and efficiency, so further tuning of this threshold would not affect our main conclusions.

**W10: The paper says that this process converge, but I don't see why (without better understanding the re-generation step)**

We thank the reviewer for raising this question. In this work, convergence refers to convergence in semantic alignment. This means that all semantic anchors become correctly represented, and this is reflected in the steady decrease in the number of misaligned anchors across iterations. At each step, SAC-Opt compares the original anchors with the anchors reconstructed from the generated code and regenerates only the ones that remain inconsistent. Anchors that are already aligned stay unchanged. This selective update focuses the process on the remaining inconsistencies and produces the progressive reduction shown in Appendix A.4, where the number of errors drops to zero in practice.

We also agree that the regeneration step benefits from clearer explanation. For each anchor, SAC-Opt first generates the corresponding code using the semantic translation step in Sec 3.3. The system then reconstructs a semantic anchor from that code following Sec. 3.4 and checks whether it matches the original anchor. If a mismatch is detected, the same generate reconstruct verify cycle is applied again to that anchor. This loop continues until alignment is achieved or the iteration limit is reached. We will expand Sec. 3 to describe this process more clearly, and Sec. 4.9 already provides a concrete example of how a single anchor is corrected through this cycle.

We can feed in the prompt to LLM-A or LLM-B. This seems trivial to me so I am not sure why the paper is making this claim. We thank the reviewer for pointing out the ambiguity in our original wording. We have revised the text to clarify that we are not referring to solver models nor claiming the existence of universal prompts. The intention was to express that this part of the analysis is important because it shows that the effectiveness of SAC-Opt does not rely on the reasoning strength of any specific LLM. Instead, the gains come from the semantic correction mechanism itself.

In Sec. 4.6, our comparison between GPT-4o and Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct serves to demonstrate this point. Although the two models differ significantly in capability, SAC-Opt consistently improves performance on both. This indicates that the method provides value beyond what the base model can achieve on its own. We have updated the paper to present this point more clearly and removed wording that may have implied a broader claim than intended.

summary.value: This paper proposes SAC-Opt, a novel framework designed to improve large language models’ (LLMs) ability to translate natural-language descriptions of optimization problems into solver-ready mathematical formulations (e.g., linear or mixed-integer programs). The key idea is the introduction of Semantic Anchors (SAs) — structured symbolic hints that connect linguistic elements (e.g., “maximum capacity”, “budget limit”) with optimization primitives (variables, constraints, and objective terms).

strengths.value:
1. Clear and Motivated Problem: The task, mapping natural-language optimization problems into executable mathematical programs, is both underexplored and highly relevant for LLM reasoning research.

2. Methodological Soundness: The two-phase design (supervised + consistency regularization) is technically reasonable and fits within modern neuro-symbolic learning trends.

3. Readable & Reproducible: Dataset and training pipeline are clearly documented.

weaknesses.value:
1. Semantic Anchors are manually curated and lack scalability: Claim of “neurosymbolic generality” (p.2, paragraph 3) is not substantiated: the current anchors are symbolic labels, not learned semantics.	There’s no automated anchor discovery or learning, which limits scalability to unseen optimization structures or domains (e.g., stochastic, nonlinear, combinatorial).

2. Anchor Consistency Loss is heuristic and lacks formal grounding: There is no analysis of failure cases where paraphrase consistency fails (e.g., negation or quantity inversion).

3.  The framework does not actually perform symbolic reasoning: Although labeled “neurosymbolic,” the framework never executes or verifies symbolic constraints during training in line 120-150. The term “neuro symbolic optimization” seems to be overstated; the system remains purely neural.

4.  Missing related work: “ReFT (Luong et al. 2024)” and “DeepSeek-RFT (2025)” are relevant to semantic alignment.

comment.value:
Dear Reviewer YBxh,

Thank you very much for taking the time to review our submission. Our work aims to address a critical gap in LLM‑based optimization modeling: **semantic errors that pass solver checks**. We propose a **training‑free**, inference‑time backward-guided correction framework that **iteratively aligns semantic anchors** (constraint/objective) reconstructed from code with those extracted from the problem description, leading to **fine‑grained semantic correction** without additional supervision.

We may be misunderstanding parts of your thoughtful comments, but several points seem to describe a different paper. Would you mind confirming whether your review was intended for our manuscript? For reference:


* **No supervised two‑phase training / no consistency regularization.** Our approach is **training‑free** (inference‑time only) follow the research line of inference framework summarized by a recent survey [1]. The Abstract explicitly states "**without requiring additional training or supervision**," and Sec. 3 / Algorithm 1 describes an iterative correction loop at inference rather than a supervised stage.
* **No "Anchor Consistency Loss."** Sec. 3.5 defines a **binary verification** $\delta$ (LLM‑based or similarity‑based) to check anchor equivalence during inference; there is **no loss function or training**.
* **No "neurosymbolic generality" / "neuro‑symbolic optimization."** Page 2, paragraph 3 explains our **core mechanism and pipeline for iterative semantic alignment**; these terms do not appear in our text.
* **Line references.** The portion cited as "during training in lines 120–150" corresponds in our PDF to **Related Work**, not a training section.
* **No "training pipeline."** We document code and evaluation for reproducibility, but there is **no training procedure** in our method or experiments.

If these remarks were indeed meant for our paper, we would be grateful for pointers to the specific passages that suggested supervised training, a loss, or the "neurosymbolic" terminology, so we can address them precisely. Otherwise, it is possible a text snippet from another submission was attached in error.

We truly appreciate your time and would welcome any technical feedback on our actual method and motivation once this is clarified. Thank you again for your careful reviewing.

Sincerely,

Authors

Reference:

[1] Xiao, Ziyang, et al. "A Survey of Optimization Modeling Meets LLMs: Progress and Future Directions." In IJCAI, 2025.

comment.value:
Dear Reviewers,

We sincerely thank all reviewers for the time, care, and expertise you invested in evaluating our work. We greatly appreciate the thoughtful comments, the recognition of the clarity and motivation of our paper, and the constructive suggestions that helped us strengthen both the technical presentation and the empirical analysis. Your feedback has substantially improved the rigor, transparency, and readability of the manuscript.

Across the reviews, the main concerns focus on the following points: (1) the significance of our semantic-anchor correction framework, (2) the clarity of the regeneration and backward verification procedure, (3) the rigor of the experimental setup, including dataset processing and statistical reporting, and (4) the completeness and accuracy of related work coverage and citations. We have carefully revised the paper to address all of these points.

* First, to clarify our contribution, we emphasize that SAC-Opt introduces  a backward semantic-level correction loop that exposes silent semantic errors that forward or solver-based pipelines cannot detect. We updated the Introduction, Related Work, and the Contributions to present this distinction clearly.

* Second, in response to questions about regeneration and convergence, we expanded Sec. 3 to describe how anchors are regenerated, reconstructed, and verified, and we highlighted in Sec. 4.7 how the correction mechanism drives practical semantic alignment.

* Third, to strengthen experimental rigor, we clarified the use of the official cleaned datasets, corrected a few results, added extended statistics in Appendix A.9, and moved key runtime analysis into the main paper to make the accuracy–runtime trade-off more transparent.

* Fourth, regarding related work and some statement, we revised terminology, added the missing citations (including Holy Grail 2.0, Ner4Opt and Text2Zinc), corrected the Pyomo statement, and refined Sec. 2 to clearly distinguish SAC-Opt from current correction methods.

We thank you again for your time reviewing our paper! We have dealt with all your concerns to the best of our ability and carefully incorporated your valuable suggestions into the updated manuscript. As the end of the author-review discussion period is approaching, we would appreciate it if you could kindly let us know whether your previous concerns have been fully addressed. We are more than happy to answer any further questions you might have.

With appreciation,

Authors

Dear Area Chair,

Thank you for the time and effort you have dedicated to evaluating our submission.

Because the discussion period ended earlier than expected, all reviewers were not able to respond to our rebuttal. To support your decision process, we summarize below the key strengths and concerns raised across all reviews, along with the clarifications made in our revision.

For **Reviewer YBxh**, we believe the comment may have been mismatched. We provided a detailed explanation in our rebuttal, though we did not receive a follow-up response.

For the remaining reviewers:

---
## **Strengths**
* Clear problem motivation and meaningful contribution to semantic correction in NL4Opt (qaYD, cmZd, yMpm)
* Clear and easy to follow presentation (qaYD, cmZd)
* Well-specified mechanism and workflow (cmZd)
* Strong empirical improvements over baselines across datasets (qaYD, cmZd)
* Useful ablations that isolate the effect of semantic correction (cmZd)
* Broad evaluation across multiple datasets and LLMs (cmZd, yMpm)
* Good reproducibility with shared code (qaYD)
---
## **Weaknesses and Our Responses**
### **Reviewer qaYD**
* The reviewer repeatedly states that they **like the paper, but argues that the contribution "fits INFORMS rather than ICLR,"** framing our semantic correction as "adding more verification," which reflects a misunderstanding of our core motivation. We clarified that our method is not about increasing verification steps but about identifying **silent semantic errors** that, to our knowledge, existing AI papers had neither recognized nor addressed prior to our work.
* The reviewer claims that the **regeneration process is unclear**; although we already provide a full algorithm, workflow diagram, and a case study; we further expanded Sec. 3 for complete clarity.
* The reviewer questions the **ordering of semantic and code verification**, but this reflects a conceptual misunderstanding: the two steps serve different purposes, and because solver execution naturally occurs at the end of the pipeline, running code verification earlier would only introduce extra cost.
* The reviewer notes a few **missing citations**, which we have added.
* The reviewer highlights **ambiguous phrasing** (e.g., "model-agnostic"), which has been corrected.
* The reviewer suggests **moving some analyses (runtime, extraction) into the main text**; we have moved the key results accordingly.
* The reviewer requests more **detailed pipeline statistics**. Such analysis exceeds the standard NL4Opt protocol followed in prior work, and we note this as future work.
---
### **Reviewer cmZd**
* The reviewer questions the strength of our **semantics-driven correction claim**. We refined the contribution wording and clarified the distinction from prior work in Sec. 2.2.
* The reviewer finds the **regeneration loop, convergence notion, and model composition** not fully specified. We expanded Sec. 3 with additional details and clarified the semantic convergence notion.
* The reviewer notes the lack of an **external semantics-anchoring baseline**, and raises concerns about **runtime and statistical robustness**. Since no prior method performs anchor-level semantic correction, such a baseline is not available. We highlighted the extended runtime and statistical analyses in the appendix and moved key results in the main text.
* The reviewer raises concerns about **extraction reliability**. We highlighted the additional discussion and manual checks in the appendix and identified extraction stress-testing as future work.
---
### **Reviewer yMpm**
* The reviewer raises concerns about **dataset sizes, data cleaning, and the validity of Table 1**, assuming that we removed data or altered benchmarks. We clarified that all datasets come directly from the official *cleaned benchmarks* released in [1]. We performed no cleaning or filtering of our own. One minor aggregation oversight in IndustryOR, which we rechecked and corrected, and the updated results do not affect any main conclusions.
* The reviewer suggests **comparisons to methods** such as LLMOPT, OptMATH, SIRL, and ORLM. Following the taxonomy of [1], these methods belong to training-based or domain-specific LLM paradigms, which differ from the inference framework setting we study. We clarified this scope distinction in the revision.
* The reviewer asks whether **iterative correction increases runtime**. We highlighted extended analysis in appendix, and we have now moved it into the main text for clearer visibility..
* The reviewer notes that **Pyomo is a modeling language rather than a solver**. We corrected this wording in the revision.

Once again, thank you for your dedication and time.

Reference:

[1] Xiao, Ziyang, et al. "A Survey of Optimization Modeling Meets LLMs: Progress and Future Directions." In IJCAI, 2025.
